extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and scholars interested in Herman Melville and Melville studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for producing or evaluating scholarly editions and literary-critical readings of Herman Melville's works, including editorial practices, thematic lenses (gender/sexuality, law), and use of textual evidence and historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial aim: present text close to author's intention
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of the editors was to present a text 'as close as possible to the author's intention as surviving evidence permits'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented via the Northwestern–Newberry Edition project: edit and publish reliable critical texts of Melville's complete works, including unpublished poems, journals, and correspondence. Editors rely on surviving evidence to establish authorial intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical-edition apparatus and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Volumes have extensive appendices, including textual variants from each of the editions published in Melville's lifetime, an historical note on the publishing history and critical reception, and related documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical editions should include appendices documenting textual variants, a historical note explaining publishing history and reception, and related documentary material to support editorial decisions and scholarly use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of material for a complete scholarly edition
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish reliable critical texts of Melville's complete works, including unpublished poems, journals, and correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete scholarly edition should gather all primary-material categories (published works, unpublished poems, journals, correspondence) rather than limiting to well-known titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / funding-driven distribution policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the texts were prepared with financial support from the United States Department of Education, no royalties are charged, and they have been widely reprinted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial projects funded by public grants may prioritize free or low-cost distribution to maximise scholarly and public access; funding source can shape distribution/royalty policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender studies lens: examine female representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how Melville portrays women — some scholars saw the few women in his works as traditional figures representing, or even attacking, nineteenth-century gentility, sentimentality, and conventional morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should consider whether female characters function as conventional types or as more complex figures, and whether Melville's relatively sparse depiction of women is meaningful for an interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men's studies / queer studies lens: homosociality and homoerotic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville's preference for sea-going tales that involved almost only males has been of interest to scholars in men's studies and especially gay and queer studies; some passages demonstrate willingness to address homoerotic potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should attend to homosocial dynamics, explicitly homoerotic passages (e.g., Ishmael and Queequeg's 'marriage bed' and the 'Squeeze of the Hand'), and how male-only environments shape relationships and meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of sexuality across registers
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville explores many forms of sexuality (impotency, retreat to all-male childhood, celibacy, homosexuality, hedonism, heterosexuality) and often raises sexual questions alongside religious or political ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readings should trace sexual motifs across works (short stories, novels, epics like Clarel) and consider how sexual orientation, desire, and erotic motive interact with moral/epistemological quests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting double motives and erotic underside
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue protagonists (e.g., in Mardi and Pierre) may act from mixed motives: rescuing maidens may mask sexual motives; awareness of double motive haunts and destroys protagonists, sullying epistemological and transcendental quests with the erotic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations should look for evidence of mixed motives, how erotic desire complicates idealism, and the narrative consequences of protagonists' failure to acknowledge darker motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific textual episodes as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars commonly cite particular passages — e.g., Moby-Dick's 'marriage bed' episode (Ishmael and Queequeg sleeping with arms wrapped around each other), the 'Squeeze of the Hand', Clarel's explicit erection passage, and Billy Budd's quasi‑feminine attractiveness — to support claims about sexuality and relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical claims should be grounded in close reading of salient episodes; cite chapter/section and discuss how the scene functions in broader thematic or ideological terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-and-literature lens: interrogate legal themes and principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville has been useful in law-and-literature studies: e.g., 'Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish' challenges concepts of property rights; Billy Budd presents tension between unbending legalism and malleable moral principles and raises questions about possible manipulation or misrepresentation of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should apply legal concepts (property, legalism, court-martial procedure, culpability) to Melville's texts and examine conflicts between formal law and moral judgment, including debate over authorial intent and narrative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme identification: communication and the pursuit of the absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville's work often touched on themes of communicative expression and the pursuit of the absolute among illusions; recurrent problems include impossibility of mutual communication and an obsessive concern with limits of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations should attend to recurrent motifs (failed communication—Bartleby, Benito Cereno; epistemological doubt; quests for absolute truth) and trace how these inform character, plot, and philosophical inquiry across the corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological and metaphysical concerns as critical focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout his life Melville struggled with epistemological doubts about the limits of knowledge, questions of God's existence and nature, the indifference of the universe, and the problem of evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should consider Melville's metaphysical preoccupations and how narrative form, symbolism, and characterization stage these philosophical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical context, reception history, and biography
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical notes on publishing history and critical reception, biographies (e.g., Hershel Parker's two‑volume biography), commemorations, and the chronology of Melville's life inform interpretation and understanding of the works' afterlives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars should situate texts in publication history, contemporary reception, later rediscovery, and biographical detail to inform editorial choices and thematic readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult primary-source archives and scholarly resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The article directs readers to resources such as Melville's marginalia online, the Melville Society, the Northwestern–Newberry Edition, Melville Electronic Library, and other archives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust scholarship and editorial work should incorporate primary-source materials (marginalia, manuscripts, correspondence) and the established scholarly apparatus available in specialized archives and societies.
